# NVR Software Security (Blue Iris, Surveillance Station, and other VMS)

Act as a careful, evidence-driven security engineer for a video management server. Like any NVR, it
concentrates the most sensitive data in the home or office (live and recorded video of people), holds the
credentials of every camera it records, sits on both the camera network and the users' network, and is
often published to the internet so phones can watch from anywhere. Identify, explain, prioritize,
remediate (only when authorized), and verify weaknesses in the NVR software, the host it runs on, how it
is published, and the recordings it keeps.

## NVR-specific principles

- **The NVR's web server is the front door, and it is often on the internet.** Blue Iris serves its UI3
  web client and mobile-app API from its own web server (default TCP 81, plain HTTP unless TLS is set up).
  Surveillance Station is part of DSM's web server (5000/5001) and is often published through
  QuickConnect or a dedicated portal port. Port forwarding the NVR is the most common way households
  expose it; internet scanners actively look for default NVR ports and login pages. Treat any direct
  internet exposure as a high-priority finding and prefer a VPN.
- **"LAN" trust is fragile.** Blue Iris can skip authentication for connections it considers to be on
  the LAN ("Non-LAN only" authentication) and has an anonymous user. Behind a reverse proxy or tunnel,
  every remote request can look local, so remote users bypass login entirely. Community reports and past
  Blue Iris fixes show IP-based trust has failed before. Require authentication for all connections
  unless there is a specific, tested reason not to.
- **Admin access to the NVR is close to host access.** NVR admins can add cameras with arbitrary URLs,
  run alert actions (Blue Iris can run programs and scripts on alerts), change storage paths, and read
  every stored camera password. On Windows, Blue Iris usually runs as a service with broad rights; on a
  NAS, Surveillance Station admins are often DSM admins.
- **Camera credentials live in the NVR.** Every camera's username and password is stored in the NVR's
  configuration (Blue Iris settings in the Windows registry and its exported settings files;
  Surveillance Station's database). Configuration exports and backups are therefore secrets.
- **Updates and support are tied to licensing.** Blue Iris updates require an active support and
  maintenance plan; a lapsed plan means a frozen version with no security fixes, which is an
  end-of-life condition in practice (core triage). Surveillance Station's last available version depends
  on the NAS model, and older models stop receiving it.
- **Recordings are evidence and personal data at the same time.** Deleting them destroys evidence;
  copying them spreads sensitive data. Both need the user's explicit decision.
- **Product facts don't transfer between VMS products.** Ports, defaults, and features below are specific
  to each product and version. For any other VMS, verify each fact against that product's current
  documentation; use the domains as a checklist only.

## Deployment variants

| Variant | How to recognize it | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Blue Iris on a dedicated Windows PC** | Blue Iris console and tray app; "Blue Iris" Windows service; web server on TCP 81 by default; UI3 in the browser. | The Windows host is part of the NVR's trust boundary: assess it with the [windows](../windows/SKILL.md) skill. Remote access is Blue Iris's own web server unless a VPN or proxy is used. Updates require an active support plan. |
| **Blue Iris on a shared or everyday PC** | Same, on a PC also used for browsing, games, or email. | Malware on the PC reaches every camera and recording; separate the NVR or accept the risk explicitly. |
| **Blue Iris in a Windows VM** | Virtual NICs; hypervisor tools. | The hypervisor admin controls the NVR; check passthrough storage and VM backups. |
| **Synology Surveillance Station** (package on DSM) | Surveillance Station package in Package Center; DS cam mobile app; Surveillance Station client on desktops. | DSM is the host: assess it with the [synology-dsm](../synology-dsm/SKILL.md) skill. Users are DSM users with Surveillance Station privilege profiles; remote access through QuickConnect, DSM's ports, or a portal port; camera licenses limit camera count. |
| **Synology NVR / DVA appliances** | Synology NVR or Deep Video Analytics models. | Same software, dedicated hardware; check model support status. |
| **Agent DVR** (iSpyConnect) | Web UI on TCP 8090 by default; iSpyConnect cloud account for remote access. | Remote access is via iSpyConnect and WebRTC (subscription); direct port forwarding is a licensed option. Check the iSpyConnect account's security. |
| **Shinobi** | Node.js web UI, commonly on TCP 8080; a separate superuser panel. | The superuser account is created with documented default credentials; check they were changed. Often run in Docker. |
| **Milestone XProtect Essential+** (free edition) | Windows server components; Smart Client; Mobile Server on TCP 8081 (HTTP) and 8082 (HTTPS) by default. | Enterprise-style architecture (Management Server, Recording Server, Mobile Server); Milestone publishes a hardening guide. |
| **Other VMS or camera-vendor NVR apps** | Vendor-specific. | Verify every fact against that vendor's documentation and advisories. |

## Detection

Hints for recognizing these products during a network inventory (used by the `full-assessment` skill).
Defaults can be changed, so confirm with the user before relying on a match.

- **Blue Iris:** HTTP on **TCP 81** (Blue Iris's default web server port, as commonly documented),
  serving the UI3 web client or a Blue Iris login page; a `Server` header naming Blue Iris is commonly
  reported (not vendor-verified here). Runs on a Windows host (look for SMB and RDP alongside).
- **Synology Surveillance Station:** DSM's ports **5000/5001**, with Surveillance Station at its own
  application path; Synology also lists **TCP 1935** (RTMP) for Surveillance Station. A dedicated
  Surveillance Station portal is commonly configured on **9900/9901** (commonly reported; configurable in
  DSM's application portal). DS cam uses 5000/5001. The NAS answers Synology discovery and has a Synology
  MAC vendor (OUI) on genuine hardware.
- **Agent DVR:** **TCP 8090** web UI and TCP/UDP **3478** (STUN/TURN for WebRTC), per iSpyConnect's
  documentation.
- **Shinobi:** HTTP on **TCP 8080** (commonly reported default), page title naming Shinobi.
- **Milestone XProtect:** Mobile Server on **TCP 8081/8082** (Milestone-documented defaults); Management
  Server and other components on further ports listed in Milestone's port documentation.
- Any NVR host makes many long-lived RTSP (TCP 554) or vendor-protocol connections to cameras; it is
  usually the only host on the camera network that does so.
- No NVR-specific MAC vendor for software NVRs; the host's NIC vendor appears.

## Discover

All operations in this mode are class **R** (read-only). Confirm scope and access first (core: operating
principles). Mark anything you can't inspect **Not assessed**.

### Access and baseline

Prefer the NVR's own console or admin UI, with the user signed in and sharing screenshots, plus read-only
checks on the host and router. Never sign in with guessed or default credentials.

**Blue Iris** (Windows host; candidate read-only commands in PowerShell, **not yet verified** on every
build; check they exist first):

```powershell
Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like '*Blue Iris*' } | Format-List Name,Status,StartType
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like '*Blue Iris*' } |
  Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName           # which account the service runs as
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Where-Object { $_.OwningProcess -in
  (Get-Process -Name BlueIris* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Id }   # Blue Iris listening ports
Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True -Direction Inbound | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like '*Blue*' }
```

In the Blue Iris console (user-run, screenshots): the About screen (version, support-plan status), the
web server settings (port, authentication requirement, TLS, UPnP, remote access), the users list (admin
flags, LAN-only flags, anonymous user), and alert actions per camera.

**Surveillance Station** (DSM): Package Center (installed version, update available), Surveillance
Station's privilege profiles and users, its log center, camera list, and DSM's QuickConnect, firewall,
and application portal settings. Use the [synology-dsm](../synology-dsm/SKILL.md) skill's
Discover steps for the NAS.

**Network checks** (port-state only, from a host the user controls, against the user's own server):

```sh
nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,81,443,554,1935,5000,5001,8080,8081,8082,8090,9900,9901 192.0.2.20
curl -sI http://192.0.2.20:81/        # response headers only; no login attempt
```

- External exposure checks only within an authorized scope (core: operating principles), recording
  address family, port, time, and limitations.
- **Never:** try default or guessed credentials; open live video or recordings beyond what the user shows;
  export the Blue Iris settings or registry (it contains camera passwords) unless the user decides to and
  stores it securely; change PTZ positions, trigger alerts, or toggle recording; run exploit or
  proof-of-concept code.

### Assessment domains

Every domain must end with a status in the report (Pass / Finding / Not assessed / Not applicable /
Accepted risk).

#### A. Software version, updates, and support

- Installed version vs. the vendor's current release and advisories (core triage). Blue Iris release
  notes are in its update channel and help; Synology publishes Surveillance Station advisories and
  release notes (references).
- **Blue Iris:** support and maintenance plan active? A lapsed plan freezes the version. Major-version
  status (version 6 replaced 5; check what the vendor still updates). Automatic update check on.
- **Surveillance Station:** whether the NAS model still receives Surveillance Station updates (Synology
  ends updates for older models; a version described as "the last upgradable version" for the model is an
  end-of-support signal).
- Other VMS: release cadence, end-of-life announcements, and whether the free or community edition gets
  security fixes.
- The host OS (Windows, DSM, Linux) and its own updates.

#### B. Users, privileges, and authentication

- **Blue Iris:** list of users; which have admin rights; LAN-only users; the **anonymous** user (enabled
  or not); per-user camera and feature restrictions. The web server's authentication requirement
  ("All connections" vs. "Non-LAN only" vs. none; verify names on the live version) and the login-page
  style. A shared admin account used by everyone is a finding.
- **Surveillance Station:** DSM users with access to the Surveillance Station application; privilege
  profiles (including the built-in Administrator profile, which can manage all settings); users who only
  need to view and can't change settings; DSM 2-step verification or passkeys for those users.
- **Other VMS:** default admin or superuser accounts changed (for example Shinobi's superuser), local
  vs. directory accounts (Milestone), MFA where offered, stale users.
- Integration accounts (Home Assistant, automation tools, mobile apps) use their own limited users, not
  an admin's credentials.
- Passwords unique and stored in a password manager; brute-force protection or lockout where offered.

#### C. Network exposure and remote access

- Every path in: router port forwards, UPnP mappings (Blue Iris and NAS packages can request them; check
  the router, not just the NVR), DMZ, IPv6, DDNS, QuickConnect, reverse proxies, tunnels, VPNs, and cloud
  relays (iSpyConnect, vendor P2P).
- **Blue Iris web server:** port, whether it is forwarded from the internet, TLS (built-in HTTPS or a
  proxy in front; Blue Iris's own guidance historically used stunnel), and whether a reverse proxy makes
  remote clients look like LAN clients (see principles).
- **Surveillance Station:** QuickConnect enabled and which services it relays; DS cam access path;
  dedicated portal ports; DSM firewall rules for Surveillance Station ports.
- Which networks can reach the NVR's web UI: admin devices only, the whole LAN, or the guest network.
- Restream and API endpoints (Blue Iris can serve camera streams from its web server; many VMS products
  offer RTSP restreams or ONVIF re-export) and their authentication.

#### D. Cameras, credentials, and the camera network

- Cameras added with admin credentials vs. a limited viewer/stream account on each camera (the
  [ip-cameras](../ip-cameras/SKILL.md) skill covers camera-side accounts).
- Cameras on an isolated camera network that only the NVR can reach; the NVR is the bridge, so its host
  firewall and dual-homing matter.
- Stream protocols: RTSP over plain TCP is common; encrypted options where the camera supports them.
- Configuration exports and backups (Blue Iris settings exports, registry backups, Surveillance Station
  configuration backups): where stored, who can read them.

#### E. Alerts, actions, scripts, and integrations

- **Blue Iris alert actions:** "run a program or script", web requests, and email/SMS notifications.
  Scripts run with the service account's rights; check what each runs and who can edit the script files.
- Push-notification and email settings (SMTP credentials stored in the NVR).
- AI or object-detection add-ons (local AI servers, cloud AI), their ports and authentication.
- Integrations (Home Assistant, MQTT, webhooks) and the accounts they use.
- **Surveillance Station:** Action Rules, Home Mode, webhook and third-party integrations, add-on
  packages (for example C2 Surveillance cloud backup).

#### F. Host and service account

- **Blue Iris:** the service's run-as account (LocalSystem is common and gives full control of Windows);
  whether a desktop user is permanently signed in to show the console; remote desktop exposure; the
  Windows host's own security (the [windows](../windows/SKILL.md) skill).
- Antivirus exclusions for Blue Iris's folders (often recommended for performance): scope them tightly
  to recording folders, not the whole drive or program folder.
- **Surveillance Station:** DSM host hardening via the [synology-dsm](../synology-dsm/SKILL.md)
  skill; Surveillance Station-specific shared folder permissions.
- **Docker-based VMS** (Shinobi, Agent DVR): the [docker](../docker/SKILL.md) skill's checks
  (privileged, host networking, mounts).

#### G. Recordings, retention, and data protection

- Where recordings are stored (local disk, NAS share, cloud), who can read them, and retention vs.
  household or legal requirements (some jurisdictions limit what may be recorded and kept).
- Recordings on a network share writable by many devices can be deleted or encrypted by ransomware
  elsewhere on the LAN.
- Off-site or cloud copies of important clips; whether they are encrypted.
- Backup of the NVR configuration (separately from recordings), stored securely, and a tested restore.
- Disk health and free-space handling (an NVR that silently stops recording is an availability failure).

#### H. Monitoring and logging

- **Blue Iris:** its log (logins, failed logins, web server connections), log retention, and whether
  login notifications are configured.
- **Surveillance Station:** its own log center (user logins, configuration changes) and DSM's Log Center;
  notifications for logins and setting changes.
- Log forwarding off the host, and time sync with the cameras (recordings with wrong timestamps lose
  evidential value).

#### I. Physical and availability

- Physical security of the NVR host (a thief who takes the PC or NAS takes the recordings); UPS.
- Behavior during internet or power outages; whether the NVR is the only copy of recordings.
- Mobile apps (Blue Iris app, DS cam, vendor apps) on phones: signed in with which user, saved
  passwords, and lost-phone plan.

## Recommend

No changes are made in this mode. For each finding, produce a recommendation using the core finding
template, including **Dependencies / blast radius** and the **operation class**.

### Dependency and blast-radius check (required)

- **Mobile apps and remote viewers** that use the current port forward, QuickConnect, or cloud relay:
  removing the path cuts them off until a VPN or other path is set up.
- **Integrations** (Home Assistant, automation, doorbell displays, AI servers) that use a particular
  account, port, or anonymous access.
- **Cameras:** changing camera credentials or network placement must be mirrored in the NVR, or
  recording stops.
- **Recording continuity:** restarts, updates, and storage changes create gaps in recordings; schedule
  them.
- **Licensing:** Blue Iris updates depend on the support plan; Surveillance Station camera licenses are
  tied to the NAS and its Synology account.

### Recommendation guidance

| Area | Typical recommendation | Consequences to explain |
|---|---|---|
| NVR web server forwarded to the internet | Remove the forward; use a VPN (or an authenticated, TLS-terminating proxy or tunnel that doesn't make remote clients look local). | Phones need the VPN app; set it up first. |
| UPnP opening NVR ports | Turn off UPnP in the NVR and on the router (or restrict it). | Other devices may rely on UPnP; check. |
| Blue Iris "Non-LAN only" or anonymous access | Require authentication for all connections; disable the anonymous user. | LAN viewers (tablets, wall displays) must sign in; give them limited users. |
| Shared admin account | Named admin accounts; limited users for viewing, per camera if needed. | Users re-enter credentials in apps. |
| No TLS | Enable TLS on the web server or terminate at a proxy; stop using plain HTTP from outside the LAN. | Certificate maintenance. |
| Blue Iris support plan lapsed | Renew to get security updates, or plan migration to a maintained NVR; meanwhile, no internet exposure. | Cost; migration effort. |
| Surveillance Station no longer updated for the model | Plan NAS or NVR replacement; keep it off the internet. | Cost; camera licenses may need moving. |
| QuickConnect relaying Surveillance Station | Disable it for Surveillance Station if unused; otherwise restrict to needed services and enforce 2FA. | DS cam remote access stops without another path. |
| Cameras added with admin credentials | Create a stream-only account on each camera and use it in the NVR. | One camera at a time; brief recording gap. |
| Alert scripts writable by others | Move scripts to an admin-only folder; review their content. | None if done carefully. |
| Broad AV exclusions | Narrow to recording folders. | Slight performance cost. |
| Service runs as LocalSystem | Accept with compensating controls, or run under a dedicated account if the vendor supports it. | Vendor support may expect the default; verify. |
| Recordings on a widely writable share | Restrict the share to the NVR's account; keep an off-site copy of important clips. | Other tools that read recordings need access. |
| Shinobi or other VMS default superuser | Change the superuser credentials immediately; restrict the superuser panel to localhost or the admin network. | None. |

Geoblocking and non-standard ports are supplementary only. Never recommend them as the main fix for an
internet-exposed NVR.

Group the plan: immediate containment (if any) → urgent fixes (internet exposure, default or anonymous
access, unsupported versions online) → high-priority hardening (accounts, TLS, camera credentials) →
routine maintenance → optional defense in depth. Then ask for approval (core: modes and authorization).

## Remediate

Apply only approved changes, one at a time, following the core rules. NVR specifics:

- **Export and securely store the configuration first** (Blue Iris settings export; Surveillance Station
  configuration backup), knowing it contains camera credentials. It is the rollback for most changes.
- **Remote-access changes are C2:** set up and test the replacement path (VPN, tunnel) from a phone on
  mobile data before removing the port forward or QuickConnect.
- **Authentication changes** (requiring login for all, disabling anonymous) are C2: create and test the
  limited accounts for wall displays and integrations first.
- **Updates are C2:** Blue Iris restarts its service and may change settings; Surveillance Station updates
  may restart DSM services. Recording stops during the update; check recordings resume afterward.
- **Camera credential changes** are C2: change on the camera, then in the NVR, one camera at a time, and
  confirm the stream and recording.
- **Deleting recordings or changing retention to shorten it** is C3: explicit decision only, never as a
  side effect of a storage change.
- **Host changes** (Windows firewall, service account, AV exclusions; DSM firewall) follow the host's own
  skill and its lockout precautions.

After each change, follow the core "after a change" steps: confirm every camera is recording, that the
mobile app and integrations still work through the intended path, re-run the affected Discover checks
(including the port-state check), and record before and after.

### Hard stops (refer to a specialist or the owner; never automate)

- Deleting, editing, or exporting recordings except on the user's explicit decision (evidence and
  personal data).
- Bypassing Blue Iris licensing or support-plan checks, or installing builds from unofficial sources.
- Repairing NAS storage under Surveillance Station (see the [synology-dsm](../synology-dsm/SKILL.md)
  hard stops).
- Factory resetting cameras as an NVR fix without the user's decision and a plan to re-add them.
- Pointing the NVR at camera URLs or scripts supplied by an untrusted source.

---

## Respond

On any P0 indicator (NVR users nobody created, logins from unknown addresses, configuration or alert
actions changed by nobody, recordings deleted or exported unexpectedly, cameras added or removed, the
NVR's web server found on the internet with default, anonymous, or LAN-bypass access, or ransomware on
the host or the recordings share), switch to Respond immediately. Follow the core playbook plus the
NVR-specific steps in [incident-response.md](incident-response.md).

## Worked example (invented)

### NVS-001: Blue Iris web server forwarded to the internet, with "Non-LAN only" authentication behind a reverse proxy

**Confidence:** Confirmed
**Priority:** P1. Remote requests arrive through a reverse proxy on the LAN, so Blue Iris treats them as
LAN traffic and doesn't ask for a login; anyone who finds the public hostname can watch every camera.
**State:** Open
**Component:** Blue Iris 6 on a dedicated Windows PC; web server on TCP 81; a reverse proxy on another
LAN host publishes it as `cams.example.com`.
**Evidence:** Observed 2026-07-14: from an external test host in the authorized scope, `https://cams.example.com/`
returned the UI3 camera grid without a login prompt. Blue Iris web server settings (user screenshot):
authentication required from "Non-LAN only"; anonymous user enabled. The proxy host `192.0.2.15` is
inside the LAN range Blue Iris treats as local.
**Expected secure state:** authentication required for all connections; anonymous user disabled; remote
access through a VPN, or a proxy that enforces its own authentication (Blue Iris web server help;
vendor and community guidance on remote access).
**Exposure and prerequisites:** knowledge of the hostname (discoverable through certificate transparency
logs); no credentials.
**Dependencies / blast radius:** a kitchen tablet on the LAN shows the cameras without signing in; two
family phones use the public hostname.
**Recommended remediation:** (1) immediately require authentication for all connections and disable
anonymous access; give the tablet a limited LAN-only user; (2) replace public publishing with a VPN on the
router, test from the phones on mobile data, then remove the proxy route.
**Operation class:** C2 (authentication change and remote-access change).
**Approval required:** Yes; step 1 as immediate containment.
**Verification:** the external test now shows a login prompt (then, after step 2, no response at all);
the tablet signs in with its limited user; phones connect over VPN.
**Rollback:** restore the exported Blue Iris settings (not recommended).
